title: Demand
summary: The law of demand says quantity demanded falls as price rises. Price changes cause movements along the curve; other determinants shift it. HL adds marginal utility and linear demand functions.

keyterms.definition: The quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at each possible price over a given time period, ceteris paribus.
As the price of a good rises, quantity demanded falls (and vice versa), ceteris paribus: an inverse relationship.
The sum of all individual consumers’ demand for a good at each price.
A change in quantity demanded caused only by a change in the good’s own price.
A change in demand at every price, caused by a change in a non-price determinant.
Goods that can be used in place of each other; a rise in the price of one raises demand for the other.
Goods used together; a rise in the price of one lowers demand for the other.
A good whose demand rises when consumer income rises.
A good whose demand falls when consumer income rises, as consumers switch to better alternatives.
When price falls, consumers’ real income rises so they can buy more of the good.
When price falls, the good becomes cheaper relative to substitutes, so consumers switch towards it.
Each extra unit consumed adds less satisfaction than the one before, so consumers pay less for extra units.
An equation Qd = a − bP, where a is quantity demanded at zero price and b gives the slope.

lessons.title: The law of demand and the demand curve

questions.prompt: Which best describes the law of demand?
options: As price rises, quantity demanded falls, ceteris paribus
As price rises, demand rises
As income rises, demand for all goods rises
As supply rises, demand rises
questions.explanation: There is an inverse relationship between a good’s price and the quantity demanded, other things equal.

questions.statement: Demand means the quantity consumers would like to buy, even if they cannot afford it.
questions.explanation: Economic demand requires both willingness AND ability to pay.

questions.text: A change in a good’s own price causes a ___ along the demand curve.
questions.explanation: Only the own price moves you along the curve; other factors shift the whole curve.

questions.prompt: Which would shift the demand curve for coffee to the right?
options: A fall in the price of coffee
A rise in the price of milk
A rise in the price of tea
A new tax on coffee producers
questions.explanation: Tea is a substitute, so dearer tea raises demand for coffee. A fall in coffee’s price is a movement; milk is a complement; a tax affects supply.

questions.prompt: The price of printers falls sharply. What happens to demand for ink cartridges?
options: It increases, because they are complements
It decreases, because they are substitutes
It is unchanged, because only own price matters
Quantity demanded of cartridges falls along the curve
questions.explanation: Cheaper printers mean more printers in use, raising demand for the complementary good, ink.

questions.prompt: Match each change to its effect on demand for a normal good, bus travel by students.
questions.explanation: Own-price changes cause movements; income, prices of related goods and the number of buyers shift the curve. Note bus travel may be inferior for some groups.

questions.statement: Market demand is found by adding individual demands horizontally at each price.
questions.explanation: At each price, the quantities demanded by every consumer are summed.

questions.text: A good whose demand falls as income rises is an ___ good.
questions.explanation: Consumers switch away from inferior goods (e.g. cheap own-brand foods) as they get richer.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a non-price determinant of demand?
options: The cost of raw materials
Tastes and preferences
Consumer income
Prices of related goods
questions.explanation: Raw material costs affect supply, not demand.

questions.prompt: A rival smartphone brand cuts its price. Order the effects on the market for Brand X phones.
items: Some consumers switch to the rival
Demand for Brand X shifts left
Brand X price and quantity fall
questions.explanation: A cheaper substitute reduces demand for Brand X; with an unchanged supply curve, its equilibrium price and quantity fall.

lessons.title: HL: utility, income and substitution effects, demand functions

questions.prompt: Why does diminishing marginal utility help explain a downward-sloping demand curve?
options: Total utility falls as more is consumed
Consumers get less extra satisfaction from each extra unit, so they will only buy more at a lower price
Firms lower prices as they produce more
Income falls as more is bought
questions.explanation: If each additional unit is worth less to the consumer, they are willing to pay less for it.

questions.statement: When the price of a normal good falls, the income and substitution effects both increase quantity demanded.
questions.explanation: Cheaper relative price (substitution) and higher real income (income effect) both raise purchases of a normal good.

questions.text: When a good becomes cheaper relative to alternatives and consumers switch towards it, this is the ___ effect.
questions.explanation: The substitution effect reflects changes in relative prices.

questions.prompt: Given Qd = 120 − 4P, what is quantity demanded when P = 10?
For Qd = 120 − 4P, at what price is quantity demanded zero?
questions.explanation: Set 0 = 120 − 4P, so P = 30. This is the vertical (price) intercept.

questions.statement: In Qd = 60 − 3P, a rise in the "a" term from 60 to 75 shows a rightward shift of demand.
questions.explanation: The "a" term captures non-price determinants; a larger value means more is demanded at every price.

questions.prompt: In Qd = a − bP, what does a larger value of b mean?
options: Demand has shifted right
Quantity demanded is more responsive to price, giving a flatter curve (P on the vertical axis)
The curve is steeper
The good is inferior
questions.explanation: b is the change in Qd per $1 change in price; a larger b means a flatter curve when price is on the vertical axis.

questions.text: Qd = 200 − 5P. If P rises from 20 to 24, quantity demanded falls by ___ units.
questions.explanation: Each $1 rise cuts Qd by 5, so a $4 rise cuts Qd by 20 (from 100 to 80).

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its description.

pairs.right: Extra satisfaction from one more unit

questions.explanation: These HL tools explain the shape and position of the demand curve.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to plot Qd = 40 − 2P on a diagram.
items: Find the Q-intercept: P = 0 gives Q = 40
Find the P-intercept: Q = 0 gives P = 20
Mark both points on the axes (P vertical, Q horizontal)
Join them with a straight line labelled D
questions.explanation: Two points are enough to draw a linear function.
